TRUSTEE COMPENSATION AND THE COURT'S REVIEW OF IT (PROB. CODE §§ 15680-15688; CAL. RULES OF COURT, RULE 7.776; THORPE V. REED; SCOTT V. MCDONALD; ESTATE OF GUMP) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for The A. L. Gump Family Trust dated June 1, 2015 · Melodie Z. Scott

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes what California law provides about the compensation of a trustee of a private express trust and about the probate court's review of that compensation — the rule that the trust instrument's own compensation terms govern; the three statutory circumstances in which a court may fix greater or lesser compensation than the instrument allows, and the prospective-only effect of such an order; the default rule of reasonable compensation when the instrument is silent; the eight factors California Rules of Court, rule 7.776, lists for determining or approving a trustee's compensation; the apportionment of compensation among cotrustees and the court's power to fix periodic compensation; the trustee's separate right to repayment of expenditures and the trustee's equitable lien; the 60-day written notice a trustee must give before charging an increased trustee's fee; the restriction on dual compensation where the trustee is an attorney or where the trustee's relatives or law firm perform legal services; the statutory petition for fixing, allowing, or reviewing the reasonableness of trustee compensation; the reduction or denial of compensation as a remedy for breach of trust, as the published decisions in Estate of Gump and Scott v. McDonald apply it; and the special compensation rules for a public guardian or public administrator serving as trustee — as background in connection with The A. L. Gump Family Trust dated June 1, 2015, of which Melodie Z. Scott is or was trustee and Danny Reed is a beneficiary, in Santa Clara County, California. It states what the statutes, the rule of court, and the published opinions say. It does not state whether any particular fee is reasonable, whether any compensation should be allowed, reduced, or denied, or what any person should do.

THE TRUST INSTRUMENT'S OWN COMPENSATION TERMS GOVERN (PROB. CODE § 15680(A))
Probate Code section 15680, subdivision (a), provides that, subject to subdivision (b) and except as provided in section 15688, a trustee is entitled to be compensated in accordance with the trust instrument if that instrument provides for the trustee's compensation. The Court of Appeal applied that rule in Thorpe v. Reed, where a special needs trust stated that a special trustee and any successor trustee "shall not be entitled to receive reasonable compensation for services in the administration of this Trust," and a professional fiduciary appointed as temporary trustee nonetheless obtained an award of fees. The court reversed and directed the trial court to deny the fee petition, describing the principle as a general one in the law of trusts and quoting Estate of Whitney for the proposition that where the creating instrument fixes the compensation of trustees they cannot claim a larger sum. Thorpe also observed that a person who considers the compensation specified in a trust inadequate could refuse to act, and held that the probate court's general statutory authority to appoint a temporary trustee under sections 15642, subdivision (e), and 17206 does not carry with it authority to compensate a temporary trustee differently from the amount the trust instrument specifies.

WHEN A COURT MAY FIX GREATER OR LESSER COMPENSATION THAN THE TRUST ALLOWS (PROB. CODE § 15680(B)-(C))
Probate Code section 15680, subdivision (b), states that upon proper showing the court may fix or allow greater or lesser compensation than could be allowed under the terms of the trust in three listed circumstances: where the duties of the trustee are substantially different from those contemplated when the trust was created; where compensation in accordance with the terms of the trust would be inequitable or unreasonably low or high; and in extraordinary circumstances calling for equitable relief. Subdivision (c) states that an order fixing or allowing greater or lesser compensation under subdivision (b) applies only prospectively to actions taken in administration of the trust after the order is made. In Scott v. McDonald the Court of Appeal described the subdivision (b)(2) circumstance — compensation that would be inequitable or unreasonably low or high — as one of the situations in which the probate court may allow greater or lesser compensation, and affirmed an order disallowing the trustee's compensation in its entirety on that footing. Thorpe v. Reed noted subdivision (c)'s prospective-only limitation in the course of holding that a trust's no-compensation clause barred the award before it.

REASONABLE COMPENSATION WHEN THE INSTRUMENT IS SILENT (PROB. CODE § 15681)
Probate Code section 15681 states that if the trust instrument does not specify the trustee's compensation, the trustee is entitled to reasonable compensation under the circumstances. The statute fixes no schedule, percentage, or hourly rate; unlike the Probate Code's separate scale for the statutory compensation of a personal representative of a decedent's estate, the trust-law rule is stated only as reasonableness under the circumstances. In Estate of Gump, decided under this article, the Court of Appeal stated that on settlement of each account a trustee is entitled to reasonable compensation for services rendered, and that the allowance of compensation rests in the sound discretion of the trial court, whose ruling will not be disturbed on appeal absent a manifest showing of abuse. Section 15682 adds that the court may fix an amount of periodic compensation under sections 15680 and 15681 to continue for as long as the court determines is proper.

THE EIGHT FACTORS A COURT MAY CONSIDER (CAL. RULES OF COURT, RULE 7.776)
California Rules of Court, rule 7.776, states that in determining or approving compensation of a trustee the court may consider, among other factors, eight listed ones: the gross income of the trust estate; the success or failure of the trustee's administration; any unusual skill, expertise, or experience brought to the trustee's work; the fidelity or disloyalty shown by the trustee; the amount of risk and responsibility assumed by the trustee; the time spent in the performance of the trustee's duties; the custom in the community where the court is located regarding compensation authorized by settlors, compensation allowed by the court, or charges of corporate trustees for trusts of similar size and complexity; and whether the work performed was routine or required more than ordinary skill or judgment. The rule was adopted as rule 7.756 effective January 1, 2003, and renumbered as rule 7.776 effective January 1, 2008. In Scott v. McDonald the Court of Appeal described the rule as providing a list of eight factors a court may consider when determining a trustee's compensation, and relied on the second factor — the success or failure of the trustee's administration — in affirming the disallowance of the trustee's fees.

APPORTIONMENT OF COMPENSATION AMONG COTRUSTEES (PROB. CODE § 15683)
Probate Code section 15683 states that, unless the trust instrument otherwise provides or the trustees otherwise agree, if the trust has two or more trustees the compensation shall be apportioned among the cotrustees according to the services rendered by them. The section is a default rule in two directions: the trust instrument may provide a different apportionment, and the cotrustees may agree to one. It addresses the division of compensation among cotrustees, not the total amount of compensation payable from the trust, which sections 15680 and 15681 govern, nor the separate question of how many trustees a trust may have or how cotrustees act together.

REPAYMENT OF EXPENDITURES AND THE TRUSTEE'S EQUITABLE LIEN (PROB. CODE §§ 15684, 15685)
Compensation for services is distinct from repayment of what a trustee has spent. Probate Code section 15684 states that a trustee is entitled to the repayment out of the trust property for expenditures that were properly incurred in the administration of the trust, and, to the extent that they benefited the trust, for expenditures that were not properly incurred in the administration of the trust. Probate Code section 15685 states that the trustee has an equitable lien on the trust property as against the beneficiary in the amount of advances, with any interest, made for the protection of the trust, and for expenses, losses, and liabilities sustained in the administration of the trust or because of ownership or control of any trust property. In Estate of Gump the Court of Appeal drew on section 15684's benefit-to-the-trust standard in reasoning about the limits of a court's discretion to disallow a trustee's compensation where the beneficiaries suffered no loss.

SIXTY DAYS' WRITTEN NOTICE BEFORE AN INCREASED TRUSTEE'S FEE (PROB. CODE § 15686)
Probate Code section 15686 defines "trustee's fee" for purposes of that section to include, but not be limited to, the trustee's periodic base fee, rate of percentage compensation, minimum fee, hourly rate, and transaction charge, while excluding fees for extraordinary services. Subdivision (b) states that a trustee shall not charge an increased trustee's fee for administration of a particular trust unless the trustee first gives at least 60 days' written notice of that increased fee to each beneficiary entitled to an account under section 16062, each beneficiary who was given the last preceding account, and each beneficiary who has made a written request to the trustee for notice of an increased trustee's fee and has given an address for receiving notice. Subdivision (c) states that if a beneficiary files a petition under section 17200 for review of the increased fee or for removal of the trustee and serves a copy on the trustee before the 60-day period expires, the increased fee does not take effect as to that trust until the court orders otherwise or the petition is dismissed.

DUAL COMPENSATION WHERE THE TRUSTEE IS AN ATTORNEY (PROB. CODE § 15687)
Probate Code section 15687, subdivision (a), states that notwithstanding any provision of a trust to the contrary, a trustee who is an attorney may receive only the trustee's compensation provided in the trust or otherwise provided in the article, or compensation for legal services performed for the trustee, unless the trustee obtains approval for the right to dual compensation as provided in subdivision (d). Subdivision (b) applies a parallel restriction to a parent, child, sibling, or spouse of a trustee and to a law partnership or corporation whose partner, shareholder, or employee serves as trustee. Subdivision (c) states that the section does not apply if the trustee is related by blood or marriage to, or is a cohabitant with, the settlor. Subdivision (d) allows approval of dual compensation, after full disclosure, either by a court order under Probate Code section 17200, subdivision (b)(21), or by 30 days' advance written notice to the persons entitled to notice under section 17203, with a petition required if a timely objection is received. Subdivision (e) states that any waiver of the section's requirements is against public policy and is void, and subdivision (f) states that the section applies to services rendered on or after January 1, 1994.

Gump Family Trust dated June 1, 2015, of which Melodie Z. Scott is or was trustee and Danny Reed is a beneficiary, in Santa Clara County, California. Probate Code section 15680, subdivision (a), provides that, subject to subdivision (b) and except as provided in section 15688, a trustee is entitled to be compensated in accordance with the trust instrument if that instrument provides for the trustee's compensation. The Court of Appeal applied that rule in Thorpe v. Reed, where a special needs trust stated that a special trustee and any successor trustee "shall not be entitled to receive reasonable compensation for services in the administration of this Trust," and a professional fiduciary appointed as temporary trustee nonetheless obtained an award of fees. The court reversed and directed the trial court to deny the fee petition, describing the principle as a general one in the law of trusts and quoting Estate of Whitney for the proposition that where the creating instrument fixes the compensation of trustees they cannot claim a larger sum. Thorpe also observed that a person who considers the compensation specified in a trust inadequate could refuse to act, and held that the probate court's general statutory authority to appoint a temporary trustee under sections 15642, subdivision (e), and 17206 does not carry with it authority to compensate a temporary trustee differently from the amount the trust instrument specifies.

expectedJSON.body: Probate Code section 16420, subdivision (a), states that if a trustee commits or threatens to commit a breach of trust, a beneficiary or cotrustee may commence a proceeding for any of the listed purposes that is appropriate, and paragraph (7) of that list is to reduce or deny compensation of the trustee. McDonald the Court of Appeal affirmed an order denying a trustee all compensation, holding that on that record the probate court could reasonably conclude that any compensation would be inequitable given the trustee's mismanagement, failure to make required court filings, and continued service while unlicensed.
